questions.q: What sigil does T-SQL require on every local variable name?
questions.explain: T-SQL local variables are always prefixed with @, e.g. @Price, which also distinguishes them from column names at a glance.

questions.q: How does PL/SQL's assignment operator differ from T-SQL's?
options: PL/SQL uses := for assignment, reserving = for comparison; T-SQL uses = (or SET ... =) for assignment
PL/SQL has no assignment operator at all
PL/SQL and T-SQL both use := identically
questions.explain: PL/SQL (and PL/pgSQL) use := for assignment and := for initialization, while T-SQL uses = in both DECLARE ... = value and SET @var = value.

questions.q: What is the genuine surprise about MySQL variables covered in this lesson?
options: MySQL has two different variable mechanisms: block-scoped DECLARE ... DEFAULT variables inside a routine, and @-prefixed session variables usable outside one
MySQL does not support variables of any kind
MySQL variables must always be declared with the @ sigil, with no exceptions
MySQL variables can only be used inside a WHERE clause
questions.explain: MySQL's DECLARE ... DEFAULT variables are scoped to a BEGIN/END block, while @-prefixed session (user-defined) variables persist for the whole client session and work outside any block.

questions.q: Where must all variables be declared in PL/SQL, compared to T-SQL?
options: In a DECLARE section before BEGIN — unlike T-SQL, which allows DECLARE anywhere in a batch
Variables can be declared anywhere in PL/SQL, just like T-SQL
PL/SQL has no concept of a declaration section
questions.explain: PL/SQL requires all variables to be declared in a DECLARE section before BEGIN, while T-SQL's DECLARE statements can appear anywhere within a batch.

questions.q: Which platform's DECLARE-section syntax most closely resembles PL/SQL's, including the use of := for initialization?
questions.explain: PL/pgSQL's DECLARE section, lack of a sigil, and := assignment are deliberately modeled on Oracle's PL/SQL.
